claim: Neuropeptide Y-expressing dorsal horn inhibitory interneurons (NPY-INs) gate spinal pain and itch signalling.
source: Neuropeptide Y-expressing dorsal horn inhibitory interneurons gate spinal pain and itch signalling
evidence: This is the main title claim of the manuscript, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the study including chemogenetic activation and silencing experiments.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of NPY-INs reduces behaviours associated with acute pain.
source: We find that chemogenetic activation of NPY-INs reduces behaviours associated with acute pain and pruritogen-evoked itch
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral testing data showing increased withdrawal thresholds and latencies.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of NPY-INs reduces behaviours associated with pruritogen-evoked itch.
source: We find that chemogenetic activation of NPY-INs reduces behaviours associated with acute pain and pruritogen-evoked itch
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by chloroquine-evoked itch behavioral data.

claim: Silencing NPY-INs causes exaggerated itch responses.
source: whereas silencing them causes exaggerated itch responses that depend on cells expressing the gastrin-releasing peptide receptor
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by TeLC-mediated silencing experiments showing increased chloroquine-evoked itch.

claim: The exaggerated itch responses caused by silencing NPY-INs depend on cells expressing the gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR).
source: whereas silencing them causes exaggerated itch responses that depend on cells expressing the gastrin-releasing peptide receptor
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing that simultaneous silencing of NPY-INs and GRPR-INs reduces the exaggerated itch response.

claim: Silencing dynorphin-expressing interneurons also increases itch, but to a lesser extent than silencing NPY-INs.
source: As predicted by our previous studies, silencing of another population of inhibitory interneurons (those expressing dynorphin) also increases itch, but to a lesser extent.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by comparative TeLC silencing experiments in PdynCre mice.

claim: NPY-IN activation reduces behavioural signs of inflammatory pain.
source: Importantly, NPY-IN activation also reduces behavioural signs of inflammatory and neuropathic pain.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by CFA-induced inflammatory pain model experiments.

claim: NPY-IN activation reduces behavioural signs of neuropathic pain.
source: Importantly, NPY-IN activation also reduces behavioural signs of inflammatory and neuropathic pain.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by SNI-induced neuropathic pain model experiments.

claim: NPY-INs represent a potential treatment target for pathological pain and itch.
source: These results demonstrate that NPY-INs gate pain and itch transmission at the spinal level, and therefore represent a potential treatment target for pathological pain and itch.
evidence: This is a concluding inference based on the experimental findings showing that NPY-IN activation suppresses pain and itch behaviors.

claim: Projection cells represent only ~1% of dorsal horn neurons.
source: However, projection cells represent only ~1% of dorsal horn neurons
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The vast majority of dorsal horn neurons comprise excitatory and inhibitory interneurons arranged into local microcircuits that process somatosensory information.
source: with the vast majority comprising excitatory and inhibitory interneurons that are arranged into local microcircuits that process somatosensory information
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Altered function of dorsal horn circuits contributes to chronic pain and pruritus (Braz et al., 2014; Cevikbas and Lerner, 2020).
source: Altered function of these circuits contributes to chronic pain and pruritus (itch) (Braz et al., 2014; Cevikbas and Lerner, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Broad disruption of spinal inhibitory signalling produces behaviours reminiscent of symptoms seen in patients suffering from chronic pain or pruritus (Beyer et al., 1985; Foster et al., 2015; Sivilotti and Woolf, 1994; Yaksh, 1989).
source: as broad disruption of spinal inhibitory signalling produces behaviours reminiscent of symptoms seen in patients suffering from chronic pain or pruritus (Beyer et al., 1985; Foster et al., 2015; Sivilotti and Woolf, 1994; Yaksh, 1989)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons in mouse superficial dorsal horn can be assigned to five largely non-overlapping populations based on expression of calretinin, parvalbumin, neuronal nitric oxide synthase, dynorphin and galanin, or neuropeptide Y (Boyle et al., 2017).
source: We have described a molecular classification scheme that assigns the inhibitory interneurons in mouse superficial dorsal horn (SDH; laminae I and II) to five largely non-overlapping populations, based on expression of calretinin (CR), parvalbumin (PV), neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS), dynorphin and galanin (Dyn/Gal), or neuropeptide Y (NPY) (Boyle et al., 2017).
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The molecular classification scheme for inhibitory interneurons has been validated and extended by large-scale transcriptomic studies (Häring et al., 2018; Sathyamurthy et al., 2018).
source: This scheme has since been validated and extended by large-scale transcriptomic studies (Häring et al., 2018; Sathyamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to independent transcriptomic studies.

claim: Molecularly defined interneuron populations display differential activation profiles in response to noxious and innocuous stimuli (Häring et al., 2018; Sathyamurthy et al., 2018; Polgár et al., 2013).

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PV interneurons are implicated in preventing tactile allodynia (Boyle et al., 2019; Petitjean et al., 2015).

However, expression was largely restricted to lamina IIo (even though many NPY cells are found in other laminae) and fewer than half of the targeted cells contained either NPY or its mRNA.
